title: Act I, Scene II
focus: Paris's suit and the Capulet invitation

teacherSummary.text: Capulet tells Paris that Juliet is too young to marry but invites him to woo her at that night's feast; her consent will count. A servant who cannot read the guest list asks Romeo for help, and Romeo learns Rosaline will attend. Benvolio urges him to go and compare her with other beauties.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “of choice / Lies my consent and fair according voice. / This night I hold an old accustom’d feast, / Whereto I have invited many” (Act I, Scene II, Capulet (speech 5)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: of choice / Lies my consent and fair according voice. / This night I hold an old accustom’d feast, / Whereto I have invited many

symbolsAndMotifs.name: fate and the stars
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: From "star-cross'd" in the Prologue to Romeo's "I defy you, stars," the lovers feel steered by fortune, while the plot shows human choices and accidents. In this scene: “At my poor house look to behold this night / Earth-treading stars that make dark heaven light: / Such comfort as do lusty young” (Act I, Scene II, Capulet (speech 5)).

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for characterization, irony (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about Paris's suit and the Capulet invitation? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act I, Scene II develops the idea of Paris's suit and the Capulet invitation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Capulet's early patience makes his later anger more shocking. When the text says “My child is yet a stranger in the world; / She hath not seen the change of fourteen years” (Act I, Scene II, Capulet (speech 3)), it shows this directly. Here he insists Juliet "hath not seen the change of fourteen years" and that "My will to her consent is but a part," words that set a standard he will later break.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
